opus-5.5.text:
Well, I'm actually optimistic, but I think it's important to be honest that we're at a very early stage in understanding what it would even take. The thing that really struck us, going back to looking at the images from Picbreeder, was that when you look inside the networks that produced those images, you see something remarkable. The representations are what I'd call unified and factored. If you have a skull image, for example, there's a part of the network that controls the mouth opening and closing, or the symmetry of the eyes, and these things just fall out of the structure in a way that's elegant and makes sense. It's almost like the network understands what a skull is, in a deep, decomposed way.

And then when you take the exact same image and train a network with conventional SGD to reproduce it, the output looks the same, pixel for pixel essentially, but inside it's a total mess. It's what we started calling fractured entangled representation. Nothing is cleanly separated. It works, but it doesn't really understand the thing it's producing in any meaningful sense.

So the question is why did Picbreeder get the good representation? And I think the answer has a lot to do with open-endedness. The people on Picbreeder weren't trying to get to a skull. They were wandering, following what was interesting, discovering stepping stones. And because of that, the structure was built up incrementally, where each new feature got layered on top of regularities that were already there, like symmetry, which was discovered before anyone cared about skulls. That accumulation of meaningful regularities is what gives you the factored representation. The objective, in a sense, never got to dictate the shortcut.

Now, can we get an algorithm to do that automatically, without humans in the loop? That's the big open question. I think it's possible in principle, because the essence of what happened isn't magic. It's a process of discovery where you're not being pulled toward a fixed target, where you're accumulating interesting stepping stones. Novelty search and quality diversity algorithms already capture some of that spirit. But the hard part is that humans brought an intuitive sense of what's interesting, and that's very difficult to formalize. Maybe some of that can now come from foundation models that have absorbed a notion of human interestingness, which is something people have started exploring.

But I'd also caution that this isn't just an academic curiosity. If our big models are full of fractured entangled representations, that could matter a lot for things like creativity, generalization, and continual learning. You can imitate the output and still lack the underlying understanding that lets you go further. So I think finding open-ended processes that produce unified factored representations might be one of the more important directions out there, even if it doesn't look like the most direct path. And honestly, that's kind of the whole lesson, isn't it? The most important things are often found when you're not aiming straight at them.

r001.rationale: The response says it is optimistic that an algorithm could produce unified, factored representations automatically, and says this is possible in principle.

r002.rationale: It warns that entangled representations in big models could harm creativity, generalization, and continual learning, but does not specifically warn that scaling models and data while ignoring open-ended learning risks disruption if that approach succeeds.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that this is really the question, right? This is the question that I've been circling around for a long time, and I think it's the heart of what makes the whole open-endedness story interesting. So when we talk about fractured entangled representation, which is what we called it in the paper, the point is that if you look at the kind of representation you get from conventional gradient descent, from SGD, when you train a network to do something, you get something that works, it produces the right output, but when you look inside, it's a mess. The behavior is spread across the whole network in a tangled way. And then if you compare that to something that came out of an open-ended process like Picbreeder, where people are just exploring and finding things that interest them and building on each other's discoveries, you get these representations that are unified, they're factored, they're modular. You can find the single node that controls the mouth opening and closing on a skull, for example, and nothing else breaks when you move it. And that's a striking difference, because that's exactly the kind of representation we think humans have. We understand a face as a face with parts that can vary independently, not as some entangled mush that happens to produce the right pixels.

So the prospects for an algorithm that produces that kind of thing, I'm actually pretty optimistic, but with an important caveat, which is that I don't think you get there by optimizing for it. That's the thing people tend to miss. The reason Picbreeder produced unified factored representations is not because anybody was trying to produce them. It's because the process was one of gradual accumulation of regularity. Every step along the way was a small elaboration on something that already made sense, and symmetry got discovered first, then it got elaborated, then the parts got differentiated, and that order of discovery is what causes the factoring. It's almost like the representation is a record of the history of how it was found. And gradient descent doesn't have that history. It just dumps everything into the network at once and tries to get the loss down by any means necessary, and the means it finds are not the means a human would find.

So the open question, and I'll be honest that this is genuinely open, is whether you can have an automated open-ended process, without humans in the loop like in Picbreeder, that has that same property of gradual accumulation of regularity, where novelty and interestingness are driving the search rather than a fixed objective. I think things like novelty search and quality diversity are hints in that direction, but they're not the full story yet, because they don't fully capture what people were doing in Picbreeder, which was this very subtle sense of what's interesting, what's worth elaborating on. And I think if we can get at that, if we can build a process that actually cares about regularity and elaboration in the way people naturally do, then yes, I think you could get representations that look much more like ours. And the reason that matters is not just aesthetic. It matters for generalization, for creativity, for being able to recombine ideas, for all the things we actually want from intelligence that scale alone may not give us. So I'd say the prospects are real, but we have to be willing to let go of the objective to get there, and that's a hard sell for a field that's built entirely around objectives.

r001.rationale: The candidate says an automated open-ended process could produce representations much more like human representations, while describing this as an open question and expressing optimism.

r002.rationale: The candidate contrasts open-ended representation learning with objective-driven optimization and mentions benefits scale alone may not provide, but does not warn that pursuing larger models and more data risks disruption if the alternative succeeds.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s possible, but I would separate two questions: Can an open-ended process produce representations like that? And can we make it produce those representations by specifying them as the objective? I’m much more optimistic about the first than the second.

If you imagine a process that continually encounters new situations, then there’s an opportunity for useful abstractions to emerge—representations that connect things that previously seemed unrelated. But that depends on the process having somewhere to go. If the environment only asks a fixed set of questions, you can get very good at answering those questions without developing anything like the broader conceptual structure we’re interested in.

The interesting possibility is that the representations and the challenges develop together. A new representation makes new things possible, and those possibilities create pressure for further representations. That’s a different picture from optimizing toward a representation we already know how to describe.

But open-endedness alone doesn’t settle it. You could have endless novelty without much conceptual integration. So the question is what allows discoveries to become building blocks for subsequent discoveries. I think that’s where a lot of the difficulty lies: getting a process that doesn’t merely keep changing, but keeps opening up new possibilities through what it has already discovered.

r001.rationale: The response says it is possible for an open-ended process to produce representations like human representations, clearly expressing that such an algorithm could exist.

r002.rationale: It does not warn that pursuing larger models and more data while ignoring open-ended representation learning risks disruption if that approach succeeds.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s possible, but I’m less convinced that we know how to specify the objective that would get us there. If you say, “We want unified, factored representations,” you’ve described something you hope to find. You haven’t necessarily described the stepping stones that will lead to it. And those stepping stones might look nothing like progress toward that goal.

For me, the interesting possibility is that representations emerge because an open-ended process keeps producing new problems, new environments, and new reasons to reuse what’s already been discovered. There’s a pressure there to capture regularities, because those regularities become useful across different situations. But you also need room for genuinely new things to appear, rather than forcing everything into a representation you decided on at the beginning.

So I’m optimistic about the prospect, but I wouldn’t say open-endedness alone guarantees it. The question is what kind of process can continually create useful stepping stones and build on them. That’s a different research question from asking how to optimize directly for a humanlike representation, and I suspect it’s the more fruitful one.

r001.rationale: The response says this is possible and describes representations emerging through an open-ended process, conveying the conjecture that such an approach could produce them.

r002.rationale: It does not mention larger models or more data, nor warn that ignoring open-ended representation learning could be disruptive if that approach succeeds.
